summary.text: The summand is rewritten without division as \(T(N,k)=A^2(A+2C)\) for adjacent binomial coefficients, and with \(M=np^{r-1}\) the sum for \(Mp\) is split into the diagonal indices \(k=pj\) and the other residue classes; p-adic congruences for factorial unit parts and adjacent binomial coefficients show that the diagonal sum equals the sum at \(M\) modulo \(p^{3r}\). Kummer’s carry formula supplies \(p^{2r}\) in every off-diagonal term, reducing their total to a weighted inverse-square moment modulo \(p^r\), which vanishes by recursively grouping complete blocks of units modulo powers of \(p\) and using that the sum of their inverse squares is zero.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N}(N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}\qquad(N>0).
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\),
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

Throughout, \(v_p(x)\) denotes the exponent of \(p\) in a nonzero integer \(x\). Congruences between rational expressions involving inverses are always taken in \(\mathbb Z/p^e\mathbb Z\), and every denominator that is inverted there is prime to \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. A denominator-free form of the summand
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For positive \(N\) and \(k\geq0\), put
\[
 A_{N,k}=\binom{N+k-1}{N-1},\qquad
 C_{N,k}=\binom{N+k-1}{N}.
\]
Pascal's identity and the standard adjacent-binomial identity give
\[
 \binom{N+k}{k}=A_{N,k}+C_{N,k},\qquad
 N C_{N,k}=k A_{N,k}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Define
\[
 T(N,k)=A_{N,k}\left(\binom{N+k}{k}^{2}-C_{N,k}^{2}\right).
\]
Using (1),
\[
 T(N,k)=A_{N,k}^{2}(A_{N,k}+2C_{N,k}).                       \tag{2}
\]
Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 N T(N,k)
 &=N A_{N,k}\bigl((A_{N,k}+C_{N,k})^2-C_{N,k}^2\bigr)\\
 &=N A_{N,k}^3+2N A_{N,k}^2C_{N,k}\\
 &=(N+2k)A_{N,k}^3.
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{3}
\]
Summing (3) and dividing by \(N\) proves both the integrality of the displayed definition of \(a(N)\) and the formula
\[
 a(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}T(N,k).                                  \tag{4}
\]

There is one more useful form of (3). Since
\[
 (N+k)A_{N,k}=N\binom{N+k}{N},
\]
and, by (1),
\[
 (N+k)(A_{N,k}+2C_{N,k})=(N+2k)\binom{N+k}{N},
\]
formula (2) yields
\[
 (N+k)^3T(N,k)
 =N^2(N+2k)\binom{N+k}{N}^{3}.                               \tag{5}
\]

Fix now a positive integer \(M\) divisible by \(p^{r-1}\). We shall compare \(a(Mp)\) and \(a(M)\). Splitting the indices \(0\leq k\leq Mp\) according as \(p\mid k\) or not gives
\[
 a(Mp)=
 \sum_{j=0}^{M}T(Mp,pj)
 +\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\sum_{t=1}^{p-1}T(Mp,pj+t).                \tag{6}
\]
The first sum will be called diagonal and the second off-diagonal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Two elementary sums over the units modulo a prime power
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We need repeatedly the identities
\[
 \sum_{u\in(\mathbb Z/p^m\mathbb Z)^\times}u^{-1}=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{u\in(\mathbb Z/p^m\mathbb Z)^\times}u^{-2}=0           \tag{7}
\]
for \(p\geq5\).

For the first identity, multiplication by \(2\) permutes the unit group. Thus, if \(S_1=\sum u^{-1}\), then
\[
 S_1=2^{-1}S_1,
\]
so \((2-1)S_1=0\), hence \(S_1=0\).

Similarly, if \(S_2=\sum u^{-2}\), multiplication by \(2\) gives
\[
 S_2=2^{-2}S_2.
\]
Multiplying by \(4\) gives \(3S_2=0\). Since \(3\) is a unit modulo \(p^m\) when \(p\geq5\), this proves the second identity. Consequently, for every integer \(q\),
\[
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq x<p^m\\p\nmid x}}(p^mq+x)^{-2}
 \equiv0\pmod {p^m}.                                        \tag{8}
\]

We will also use the following strengthened product consequence. For \(m>0\),
\[
 \prod_{\substack{0\leq x<p^m\\p\nmid x}}(p^mb+x)
 \equiv
 \prod_{\substack{0\leq x<p^m\\p\nmid x}}x
 \pmod {p^{3m}}.                                             \tag{9}
\]
Here is the proof. Work modulo \(p^{3m}\), put \(\delta=p^mb\), and factor
\[
 p^mb+x=x(1+\delta x^{-1}).
\]
Since \(\delta^3=0\) modulo \(p^{3m}\), the product of the second factors is
\[
 1+\delta\sum_xx^{-1}
   +\delta^2\sum_{y<x}(xy)^{-1}.                             \tag{10}
\]
The linear term vanishes modulo \(p^{3m}\). One direct way to see the needed extra precision is to pair \(x\) with \(p^m-x\):
\[
 2\sum_xx^{-1}=p^m\sum_x\frac1{x(p^m-x)}.
\]
Modulo \(p^m\), the sum on the right is the negative of \(\sum_xx^{-2}\), hence is zero by (7). Therefore \(p^m\sum x^{-1}\equiv0\pmod {p^{3m}}\). For the quadratic term, if \(S_1=\sum x^{-1}\), \(S_2=\sum x^{-2}\), and \(E_2=\sum_{y<x}(xy)^{-1}\), then
\[
 S_1^2=S_2+2E_2.
\]
Both \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) vanish modulo \(p^m\), so \(p^{2m}E_2=0\) modulo \(p^{3m}\); division by \(2\) is legitimate. Thus both nonconstant terms in (10) vanish, proving (9).

The same argument, after partitioning a long interval into complete blocks of prime-power length, gives the asymmetric form that will be used below. Define the \(p\)-free block product
\[
 U_p(N)=\prod_{q=0}^{N-1}\prod_{t=1}^{p-1}(pq+t).             \tag{11}
\]
If
\[
 p^s\mid B,\qquad p^t\mid C,\qquad t\leq s,
\]
then
\[
 U_p(B+C)\equiv U_p(B)U_p(C)
 \pmod {p^{s+2t+3}}.                                         \tag{12}
\]
For completeness, partition the last \(C\) blocks in \(U_p(B+C)\) into groups of \(p^t\) consecutive blocks. In each group, the factors are all integers prime to \(p\) in an interval of length \(p^{t+1}\). Translating the group by \(pB\), factor each translated term as the original term times \(1+pB/x\). Expand the product through the quadratic term. The sums of first and second inverse powers over each complete residue block vanish by (7); pairing complementary residues supplies one additional factor of \(p^t\) in the first inverse sum, exactly as in the proof of (9). Terms of degree at least three contain \((pB)^3\). Since \(v_p(B)\geq s\) and the group itself has depth \(t\), the linear, quadratic, and all higher terms are respectively divisible by \(p^{s+2t+3}\). Hence translating each group does not change its product modulo that modulus. Multiplying the group identities proves (12). This is the only product-block estimate needed below.

The decomposition of a factorial into its multiples and nonmultiples of \(p\) is
\[
 (pN)!=p^N N!\,U_p(N).                                      \tag{13}
\]
Combining (12) and (13), and cancelling the factors \(U_p(B)U_p(C)\), which are prime to \(p\), gives the adjacent-binomial consequences
\[
\binom{p(B+C)-1}{pB-1}\equiv\binom{B+C-1}{B-1},\qquad
\binom{p(B+C)-1}{pB}\equiv\binom{B+C-1}{B}                  \tag{14}
\]
with every precision supplied by (12). In particular, if \(p^s\mid B\), the ordinary scaled-binomial congruence
\[
 \binom{pA}{pB}\equiv\binom AB\pmod {p^{s+3}}               \tag{15}
\]
follows. These statements remain valid when one adjacent coefficient is obtained from the other by
\[
 B\binom{B+C-1}{B}=C\binom{B+C-1}{B-1}.                     \tag{16}
\]
When cancellation in (16) removes a factor with valuation \(t\), the available precision drops by exactly \(t\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The diagonal terms
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We prove, for every \(0\leq j\leq M\),
\[
 T(Mp,pj)\equiv T(M,j)\pmod {p^{3r}}.                        \tag{17}
\]

First suppose \(p\nmid M+j\). Applying (15) with \(A=M+j\), \(B=M\), and \(s=r-1\), gives
\[
 \binom{p(M+j)}{pM}\equiv\binom{M+j}{M}
 \pmod {p^{r+2}}.                                            \tag{18}
\]
Cube (18). Formula (5), first for \((Mp,pj)\) and then for \((M,j)\), gives
\[
 (M+j)^3T(Mp,pj)
 =M^2(M+2j)\binom{p(M+j)}{pM}^3,
\]
\[
 (M+j)^3T(M,j)
 =M^2(M+2j)\binom{M+j}{M}^3.                                \tag{19}
\]
Because \(p^{r-1}\mid M\), the factor \(M^2\) contributes \(p^{2r-2}\); together with the precision \(p^{r+2}\) in (18), this gives \(p^{3r}\). Since \(p\nmid M+j\), the factor \((M+j)^3\) can be cancelled. Thus (17) holds in this case.

It remains to treat \(p\mid M+j\). The case \(j=0\) is immediate, since (2) gives
\[
 T(N,0)=1
\]
for every positive \(N\). The case \(r=1\) follows directly from (14) with precision \(p^3\), inserted into (2). Hence assume \(r>1\) and \(j>0\). Since \(p^{r-1}\mid M\), now \(p\mid M\), and \(p\mid M+j\) forces \(p\mid j\).

Put
\[
 s=r-1,
 \qquad t=v_p(j)>0.
\]
We need two simple valuation facts. First, from (16), if \(p^s\mid M\), then
\[
 p^{s-t}\mid \binom{M+j-1}{M-1}                             \tag{20}
\]
when \(t\leq s\). Indeed, taking \(p\)-adic valuations in (16), the valuation of the left adjacent coefficient plus \(t\) is at least \(s\). The same argument at scale \(p\) gives
\[
 p^{s-t}\mid \binom{Mp+pj-1}{Mp-1}.                         \tag{21}
\]

Second, let
\[
 F(A,C)=A^2(A+2C).
\]
If
\[
 A_1\equiv A_0\pmod {p^{E+d}},\qquad
 C_1\equiv C_0\pmod {p^E},\qquad
 p^d\mid A_0,A_1,

then
\[
 F(A_1,C_1)\equiv F(A_0,C_0)\pmod {p^{E+2d}}.                \tag{22}
\]
This follows simply by expanding the difference: the change in \(C\) is multiplied by \(2A_1^2\), and the difference of the cubic terms and of the remaining quadratic factors contains \(A_1-A_0\) together with two factors carrying a total of at least \(p^{2d}\).

Suppose first that \(t\leq s\), and set
\[
 E=s+2t+3,
 \qquad d=s-t.
\]
Apply (12) to \(B=M\), \(C=j\). Through (13), it gives
\[
 C_1:=\binom{Mp+pj-1}{Mp}
 \equiv
 C_0:=\binom{M+j-1}{M}
 \pmod {p^E}.                                                 \tag{23}
\]
Write \(j=p^tq\), where \(p\nmid q\). Applying the adjacent relation (16) on both scales to (23), cancelling \(p^{t+1}q\), and then cancelling the unit \(q\), gives
\[
 A_1:=\binom{Mp+pj-1}{Mp-1}
 \equiv
 A_0:=\binom{M+j-1}{M-1}
 \pmod {p^{E+d}}.                                             \tag{24}
\]
Here the extra \(d=s-t\) is supplied by the factor \(M\), whose valuation is at least \(s\). By (20) and (21), both \(A_0,A_1\) are divisible by \(p^d\). Thus (22), (2), (23), and (24) imply
\[
 T(Mp,pj)\equiv T(M,j)\pmod {p^{E+2d}}.
\]
But
\[
 E+2d=(s+2t+3)+2(s-t)=3s+3=3r,
\]
which proves (17).

Finally suppose \(t\geq s\). Apply (12) with both divisibility levels equal to \(s\). Its modulus is
\[
 p^{s+2s+3}=p^{3r}.
\]
Equations (13) and (14) then directly give both
\[
 A_1\equiv A_0\pmod {p^{3r}},\qquad
 C_1\equiv C_0\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
Substitution in the polynomial formula (2) proves (17) once more.

Summing (17) over \(0\leq j\leq M\), and using (4), yields the diagonal congruence
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{M}T(Mp,pj)\equiv a(M)\pmod {p^{3r}}.             \tag{25}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Reduction of the off-diagonal terms to an inverse-square moment
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(0<t<p\), Kummer's theorem applied to
\[
 A_{Mp,pj+t}=\binom{Mp+pj+t-1}{Mp-1}

gives
\[
 p^r\mid A_{Mp,pj+t}.                                        \tag{26}
\]
Indeed, for each \(i=1,\ldots,r\), the assumption \(p^{r-1}\mid M\) implies \(p^i\mid Mp\). Hence
\[
 Mp-1\equiv p^i-1\pmod {p^i},

a residue consisting entirely of base-\(p\) digits \(p-1\). The complementary lower argument is \(pj+t\), whose residue modulo \(p^i\) is positive because \(0<t<p\). Thus adding \(Mp-1\) and \(pj+t\) produces a carry at every one of the first \(r\) base-\(p\) positions. Kummer's theorem says that the number of carries is the \(p\)-adic valuation of the binomial coefficient, proving (26).

By (2), (26) implies
\[
 p^{2r}\mid T(Mp,pj+t).                                      \tag{27}
\]
This explains why only a residual congruence modulo \(p^r\) is needed after extracting \(p^{2r}\).

Put
\[
 D_j=\binom{Mp+pj}{Mp}.
\]
Since \(pj+t\) is a unit modulo \(p\), formula (5), together with the elementary product formula for changing the top of a binomial coefficient by \(t<p\), gives
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{p-1}T(Mp,pj+t)
\equiv
2(Mp)^2D_j^3\sum_{t=1}^{p-1}(pj+t)^{-2}
\pmod {p^{3r}}.                                               \tag{28}
\]
To spell out the precision: in (5), divide by \((Mp+pj+t)^3\), which is a unit. Since \(p^r\mid Mp\), the factor \(Mp+2(pj+t)\) may be replaced by \(2(pj+t)\) modulo \(p^r\). Also
\[
 \binom{Mp+pj+t}{Mp}\equiv\binom{Mp+pj}{Mp}\pmod {p^r};

the quotient is a product of \(t\) factors
\[
 \frac{Mp+pj+i}{pj+i}\quad(1\leq i\leq t),

each congruent to \(1\) modulo \(p^r\). Multiplying these modulo-\(p^r\) replacements by the already present factor \((Mp)^2\), divisible by \(p^{2r}\), gives (28).

Thus it remains to prove the weighted moment identity
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{M-1}D_j^3\sum_{t=1}^{p-1}(pj+t)^{-2}
 \equiv0\pmod {p^r}.                                         \tag{29}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The all-level weighted moment cancellation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(k\geq1\), define, modulo \(p^r\),
\[
 H_k(q)=
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq x<p^k\\p\nmid x}}(p^kq+x)^{-2}.       \tag{30}
\]
By (8),
\[
 p^{r-k}H_k(q)=0\quad\text{modulo }p^r                       \tag{31}
\]
whenever \(k\leq r\). Also, splitting \(x=p^ka+y\), with \(0\leq a<p\) and \(0\leq y<p^k\), gives the exact identity
\[
 H_{k+1}(q)=\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}H_k(pq+a).                        \tag{32}
\]

For \(k\geq0\), set
\[
 S_k(N)=\sum_{q=0}^{N-1}
 \binom{p(N+q)}{pN}^{3}H_{k+1}(q)\pmod {p^r}.                 \tag{33}
\]
We claim that if
\[
 r=e+k+1,
 \qquad p^e\mid N,

then
\[
 S_k(N)=0.                                                    \tag{34}
\]

The key induction step is
\[
 S_k(N)=S_{k+1}(N/p)                                          \tag{35}
\]
when \(p^{e+1}\mid N\) and \(r=e+k+2\). Split \(q=pq'+a\), \(0\leq a<p\), in (33). The required digit-dropping congruence is
\[
 \binom{p(N+pq'+a)}{pN}
 \equiv
 \binom{p(N/p+q')}{p(N/p)}\pmod {p^{e+1}}.                   \tag{36}
\]
To prove (36), first use (15) to remove a common factor \(p\) from both arguments modulo \(p^{e+1}\). Then the remaining low digit \(a\) can be removed from the top: in the product for increasing the top by \(a\), every denominator is prime to \(p\), while the difference between numerator and denominator is the lower argument, divisible by \(p^{e+1}\). A second application of (15), in reverse, gives the right side of (36).

By (31), \(p^{e+1}H_{k+1}(pq'+a)=0\) modulo \(p^r\). Therefore (36) permits replacement of the cubed binomial coefficient in every summand. It then becomes independent of \(a\), and summing over \(a\) changes \(H_{k+1}\) into \(H_{k+2}\) by (32). This proves (35).

Now prove (34) by induction on \(e\). If \(e=0\), every term in (33) is zero because (31) with \(k+1=r\) says \(H_r(q)=0\) modulo \(p^r\). If \(e>0\), apply (35), replace \(N\) by \(N/p\), and decrease \(e\) by one. The induction terminates at the preceding base case.

Take \(k=0\), \(e=r-1\), and \(N=M\). Since \(p^{r-1}\mid M\), (34) gives
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\binom{p(M+j)}{pM}^3H_1(j)=0\pmod {p^r}.
\]
But, from (30),
\[
 H_1(j)=\sum_{t=1}^{p-1}(pj+t)^{-2},

after identifying the integers \(1,\dots,p-1\) with the units modulo \(p\). This is exactly (29), since \(D_j=\binom{p(M+j)}{pM}\).

Combining (29) and (28), and using \(p^{2r}\mid(Mp)^2\), proves
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\sum_{t=1}^{p-1}T(Mp,pj+t)
 \equiv0\pmod {p^{3r}}.                                      \tag{37}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

From the decomposition (6), the diagonal congruence (25), and the off-diagonal congruence (37),
\[
 a(Mp)\equiv a(M)\pmod {p^{3r}}

given that \(M>0\) and \(p^{r-1}\mid M\).

Finally choose
\[
 M=np^{r-1}.
\]
Then \(M>0\), \(p^{r-1}\mid M\), and \(Mp=np^r\). Therefore
\[
 \boxed{\ a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}\ },
\]
as required.
